Operator
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to Siemens Energy AG's Q3 for fiscal 2025. Welcome to our conference call. All of the participants are in listener mode, and this call will be recorded. After the presentation, you will be able to ask questions. If you want to ask a question, please press asterisk 1 on your phone. If you need help from an operator during the call, please press asterisk 0 on your phone. I'd now like to hand over to the moderator, Tim Proll-Gerwe.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Good morning and welcome to today's conference call for the Q3 at Siemens Energy. We published our financial figures at 7:00 AM this morning, and we'd like to give you an overview of that right now. We are in Berlin. In addition to Christian Bruch, we have the CFO, Maria Ferraro.
They are both here to answer your questions at the end of the presentation. Mr. Bruch will be speaking in German, and Ms. Ferraro in her mother tongue, English. We have two webcasts, an original line and an English line, where interpreters will be interpreting from German into English. For questions, journalists were able to register ahead of time with a separate telephone number. We sent you the link with the invitation to today's call. Of course, you can still register today now by dialing in. In the chat, you can also ask your questions. We've seen that there are a number of investors who have already asked questions. The investor call will be after this call. This call is for journalists only. To avoid any feedback, I'd like to ask that you put your phones on mute.
The presentations can be downloaded on our website after the call. You will also have additional slides with additional financial figures. Please remember that there is no text on the website. Both speakers will be speaking freely. Of course, there is the recording. I'd like to remind you of our Safe Harbor Statement and our forward-looking statements, which are on the second page of our quarterly presentation. Right, Mr. Bruch, you might think it's finally a boring quarter. You replaced the counter-guarantees, and then the share price went up to over EUR 100. We're not all that boring after all. Over to you now.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Well, thank you very much, Tim. Good morning to all of you. Thank you for joining us today. As usual, what I'm going to do is I'm going to give you an overview of our developments in the past quarter. After that overview, Maria will then go into the details of the figures. Basically, I can only repeat what I already said in Q2. Yes, it may be boring. Despite the geopolitical challenges, we continue to operate in what is an attractive market environment. The rising electricity demand and the need to replace aging infrastructure are indeed ensuring a sustained high demand for our solutions. I will come back to the situation in the United States, and especially the current tariff agreement between the U.S. and the EU. I'll do that in a moment.
I will also say a few words about our capacity expansions and our investments a little later. Now, Q3 was the most successful quarter in Siemens Energy's 5-year history in terms of order intake. Our customers placed orders for products and services worth EUR 16.6 billion, which exceeded the order intake for the same quarter of the last year, about almost 65% adjusted for currency and portfolio effects. All segments contributed to this very good order intake. I want to highlight, in particular, Siemens Gamesa's two major offshore orders in the Polish Baltic Sea, worth a total of over EUR 3 billion. I'd like to take this opportunity here to thank more than 100,000 colleagues who work very hard every day to serve our customers.
Our order backlog is now at a new high of EUR 136 billion, which is all the more remarkable if you bear in mind that we had to put up with negative currency effects of about EUR 4 billion to do the current strength of the euro. This order backlog gives us planning certainty. That's important for us, always important, because the order situation can fluctuate from quarter to quarter. Ultimately, it is about sustainable. It's about profitable growth. We're currently investing heavily in this, and we're developing our workforce. As I said in a moment, I'm going to give you an overview. On a comparable basis, with the same quarter last year, we increased revenue by 13.5% to EUR 9.7 billion in Q3. The profit margin before special items was 5.1%. The bottom line for Q3 was a profit after taxes of EUR 697 million.
We're on track to meet our revised forecast. We're currently aiming to reach the upper end of the target range. Now, in this, our focus remains on profitable growth. We're focusing on 3 things. We need to create the conditions for growth. We want to continuously improve profitability and strengthen our portfolio. We're making discernible progress in this regard, step by step. We resume sales activities for the revised 4.X turbine in September 2024. In wind, we now have also started sales activities for the revised 5.X turbine. This turbine has undergone a fundamental technical overhaul. We're now starting sales with an initially limited number of units. You can expect that it will take some time before the projects based on this turbine become visible in our order intake. Really, that is the usual sequence of project development in the wind business.
With that strong growth, the robustness of our supply chain is very important for us. This is especially true in this geopolitically volatility. In the past quarter, we signed a letter of intent with Japanese company TDK for the supply of rare-earth magnets. Now, these magnets are particularly important for those large offshore wind turbines. Today, they're sourced almost exclusively from China. In this quarter, an important step was the replacement of the federal government's counter-guarantees with an agreement with our commercial banks. I'm really proud that we were able to achieve this ahead of schedule. The German Bundestag's Budget Committee has taken a decision on 30 July. Now the basis has been laid for us to pay our shareholders a dividend for the current fiscal year if the AGM next year agrees. Now, Maria, in a moment, will give you some more details.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the German government for their support. Now, in the current market environment, we are continuously developing our portfolio. These are first of all steps to increase capacity or secure supply chains. For example, we have acquired our remaining 50% of the former joint venture RWG. RWG is a company that exclusively performs maintenance and repairs for smaller gas turbines from Siemens Energy. The company generates sales of just over EUR 200 million. We expect this transaction to close at the end of the year. Now, when it comes to partnerships, I'd like to once again highlight our cooperation with Rolls-Royce in Small Modular Reactors. Now, we do not expect the technology to be ready for the market until after 2030. However, we're already laying the foundations now to participate in future growth markets.
Our partner, Rolls-Royce, has already been commissioned by Great British Nuclear to build 3 of those SMRs in the U.K.. We would contribute the conventional part to that. We're also well positioned here. The United States is the world's largest energy market. Well, for this reason, I'd like to comment on developments there separately. Of course, first of all, there's the tariff situation. I welcome that there's an agreement between the U.S. and the European Union so that at least provides some planning certainty. Now, the unilateral introduction of 15% tariffs is a significant step. We would naturally have preferred to avoid that. In Q3, 35% of our orders came from the U.S.. For Gas Services, this figure was even higher at about 50%. Still, you have to take a differentiated view here.
On the one hand, we are manufacturing locally in the U.S.. On the other hand, we also have international supply chains in the sense that we're not just importing from the EU. Many details regarding the tariff situation still need to be clarified so we can, at this moment, only estimate the final impact on us. By Q3 of the year, we had incurred customs duties of around EUR 100 million. In Q4, we would expect an additional mid-double-digit million EUR amount. Now, given the current agreement between the EU and the U.S., that figure is slightly higher than originally assumed. These charges are primarily related to our Rolls-Royce service contracts, where those charges cannot simply be passed on to customers. Now, given the good, strong operating performance, we can compensate for the additional burden. It is still a painful process.
For new and existing delivery projects, we're normally in a situation where we can pass on the tariffs to our customers. Despite the tariff situation, we're currently seeing an extremely strong market in the United States for energy solutions. Both in terms of the replacement of outdated infrastructure and the enormous demand for electricity for data centers, in particular, are now driving very high demand for our products in the U.S.. Gas Services, for example, have secured gas turbine orders totaling 14 GW in the fiscal year to date. 60% of those are for data centers. Grid Technologies reserved an order in Q3 for a high-voltage direct current transmission system for the low-loss transport of large amounts of electricity and has also received several orders for transformers, both of which are critical infrastructure products.
In the onshore wind sector, we have, once again, received orders for repowering, which is the replacement of existing, older units. Order intake in the United States amounted to around EUR 5.8 billion in Q3, in other words, tripling compared with the same quarter last year. In the current market environment, it is important to me to point out that we maintain a broad global footprint in terms of order intake. We have, once again, succeeded in securing important orders in various regions this quarter. Now, Europe is and remains a key market for us. Investment in grid infrastructure is a major driver here in Europe, benefiting our Grid Technologies business segment. We currently continue to be positive about the investment activity in this segment here in Europe.
For example, National Grid and ScottishPower in the U.K. want us to be their preferred supplier for those two major HVDC projects. The Middle East, like Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates, also continue to be an important sales market for us. In the Transformation of Industry segment, we received many orders from Northern Europe, from Asia, and Australia, resulting in a 23% increase in order intake compared with the same quarter last year. To sum this up, let me say once again, we had a strong quarter with a record order intake. We are working through our plan now step by step. We're making good progress. The tariffs are having an impact on our business. We currently expect that this impact is manageable because, at the end of the day, our business is so broadly positioned that we can have spread those risks well.
With that, you are now going to hear more detailed figures from Maria. Please.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Thank you, Christian. Good morning, everyone. A warm welcome also from my side. Thank you for joining us. Let's start with an overview of our financial performance for Q3 at group level. As you see here, orders grew by 65% on a comparable basis. There's one thing that I would like to point out, which is that due to the strong euro, we've had some headwinds from currency translation and foreign exchange effects, which, in essence, means we have a bigger spread than usual between nominal and comparable growth. You'll see that here. In terms of order growth, that was spread across all business areas, also driven by Siemens Gamesa, as mentioned, where we booked 2 large offshore orders, each worth more than EUR 1.5 billion. Book-to-bill ratio remains strong at 1.7.
This is driving our order backlog to another record high of EUR 136 billion, continuing to provide us transparency for the future and to provide a strong foundation not only for this year but also for midterm targets. Looking at revenue, here we rose by 13.5% and reached EUR 9.7 billion. The growth in revenue was primarily driven by Grid Technologies, which grew by 26%, and Gas Services, which grew by 17%, again, both on a comparable basis. Profit before special items increased quite significantly, almost 10 times year-over-year, to EUR 497 million. Here, all segments increased sharply, of course. For Siemens Gamesa, it was as expected in the quarter. Profit increase was mainly due to increased volume and corresponding fixed cost absorption effects. Of course, we continue to execute through our high-margin projects.
This is driven by better pricing and a strong service contribution of 33% in the quarter. Looking at special items this quarter, as expected, the demerger of Siemens Energy India Ltd, this led to an effect of roughly positive EUR 0.5 billion and resulted in a profit of EUR 956 million for the quarter. Just as a refresher, on 9 June, Siemens Energy India Ltd was successfully listed. As we've said before, our aim is to become the major shareholder in 2028. We will achieve this by swapping the 6% ownership of Siemens India Limited and purchasing the remainder from Siemens AG. The required cash out for this will fluctuate with the relative share price developments of both and is included in our business plan for 2028. Of course, this depends on the share price of Siemens Energy India Ltd in 2028 accordingly.
Our free cash flow this quarter was EUR 419 million, around EUR 300 million lower than in Q3 of prior year. Again, this is mainly due to a few things. One, we've had shifts to Q4. Also, we have changes in our operating net working capital. This is driven mainly by a reduction of trade payables as well as a lower increase in contract liabilities. This is mainly in Siemens Gamesa. Overall, though, as expected for the quarter. Now, let's take a brief look at the performance of our business areas on the next page. Again, please refer to our website for the complete breakdown by business area. Looking at Gas Services, we had a very strong quarter, once again benefiting, as Christian mentioned, from a very strong gas market with EUR 6.3 billion in order intake. This is another record order backlog for Gas Services, which now stands at EUR 53 billion.
Looking at revenue, this stood at EUR 3.1 billion for Gas Services. This is just shy of a 17% increase on a comparable basis. Q3 profit before special items was EUR 406 million. This is nearly double year-over-year and has resulted in a margin of 13%. Overall, a very strong quarter for Gas Services. Now, looking at Grid Technologies, also with a very strong Q3, orders at EUR 4.2 billion for Grid Technologies. This is up 24% year-over-year and driven, again, as Christian mentioned, by the strong broad-based demand across products, excuse me, and solutions, as well as across different regions. The order backlog for GT stood at EUR 38 billion. Revenue grew by 26% on a comparable basis. This is substantial growth. This was driven, again, by increase in both the products and solutions businesses within Grid Technologies.
Profit before special items was at EUR 448 million, almost double compared to last year. This resulted in a margin of 15.9%. Again, this improvement in profit was driven by strong underlying operational performance. Overall, a very strong quarter for our GT business. Moving on to Transformation of Industry, Q3 orders at EUR 1.4 billion. This is a 23.4% increase driven by new unit orders therein, with an increase of 35%. Revenue for Transformation of Industry grew by 5.1% comparable, this driven by all business, with our compression business being the biggest contributor. Q3 profit before special items was at EUR 157 million, again, an increase of roughly 50% compared to prior year, with a margin of 11.5%. Here, profit was driven by sustained volume growth, particularly in service. For Siemens Gamesa in Q3, we had an extremely strong order intake with all other KPIs, as mentioned earlier, in line with expectations.
As you know, the business is still in restructuring or transformation mode, which means some variability quarter to quarter. For example, the first half of this fiscal year was trending positively versus prior year. However, in Q3, for example, operational improvements were offset mainly by 2 effects. One, the tariff impact. Here, the business was impacted with a mid-double-digit EUR amount. This is mainly due to catch-up effects on contracts and, in some cases, one-time in nature. Secondly, in Q3, we perform, and Siemens Gamesa, the regular annual update of the statistical models. This is utilized for the evaluation of the entire wind turbine fleet with respect to failure rates and cost assumptions. This caused also a high double-digit million EUR amount, again, well within our expectations. Also, maybe to note, our 4X and 5X provisions here remained basically stable.
Again, overall, a strong or as expected quarter for our businesses. Now moving on to our net cash position. With respect to net cash, here you see, overall, we have a strong cash position with EUR 8.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Our financial debt reduced slightly to EUR 3.7 billion, of which EUR 2.2 billion is long term. Considering also pension provisions, taking that into account, this brings us into an adjusted net cash position of EUR 4.4 billion at the end of June. Again, for comparison, just a year ago, we were at EUR 1.7 billion. With this, we continue to have a strong balance sheet, commensurate with our investment grade profile, which is also reflected in our external ratings. A perfect segue to the next slide.
Here you see, during this quarter, we also had several milestones, which is building a strong financial foundation, excuse me, for us. On 5 June, we announced the replacement of the EUR 11 billion facility backed by the German federal government and the EUR 1 billion facility backed by Siemens AG. Now we have a new EUR 9 billion syndicated facility, which fully supports our large-scale projects business and guaranteed demands for the years to come. This achievement relieves us of a financial burden. As you recall, we did have a cost for the Bund-backed facility of approximately EUR 100 million plus in the fiscal year of 2026. On 9 June, Siemens Energy India Ltd, as I mentioned, in India, this was also successfully listed on the Indian Stock Exchange. On 26 May 2025, S&P revised their outlook for us to positive from stable and affirmed the BBB- rating.
On 17 June 2025, we received an investment grade rating of Baa2 with a positive outlook in its inaugural rating from Moody's. Finally, last but not least, thanks to replacing our federal counter-guarantees ahead of time, we have created the foundational conditions for enabling dividend distributions to our shareholder as the dividend restriction was lifted, as mentioned earlier. Again, this was just the first step. Now, with respect to the dividend, we have to complete the fiscal year as planned so that we can, with approval of the supervisory board, recommend a dividend payment for the shareholders to vote on at our next annual shareholder meeting in February 2026. Just a gentle reminder that our dividend policy is to distribute between 40% and 60% of net income attributable to shareholders. Now, moving on to our outlook.
As you recall, we last upgraded our guidance in our Q2 financial disclosure. Today, we are reaffirming that guidance. We are currently trending towards the upper end of those ranges. Again, this includes the already mentioned direct impact from tariffs after mitigation measures of around EUR 100 million stemming from global impact of tariffs, also including China and specific raw material tariffs. Based on the recent EU-U.S. agreement of 15% tariffs effective from July, we now expect a further negative profit impact of up to a mid-double-digit million EUR amount in Q4. This brings the total estimated impact on Siemens Energy to approximately EUR 150 million, as mentioned by Christian. Please note that this effect is already embedded in our guidance.
In November, we will give you an update of our midterm card targets with the full year results and, of course, then thereafter on our Capital Market Day. With that concludes my portion of the presentation. I hand back over to you, Christian. Thank you.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Ja, vielen Dank, Maria.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Thank you very much, Maria. As I said, I'm going to say something about our investments and expansions. We are growing, as you've seen in our numbers, significantly. We're continuously investing in the locations. We're hiring new employees this year. Our investments are almost EUR 2 billion globally. We're also investing in Germany. It's important to me to talk about this. Things are happening here. We at Siemens Energy are also supportive of the Made in Germany initiative. I think it is important that we highlight those positive developments here.
We want to restore public confidence in the future. We want to send a signal, encourage people to tackle the things we need to improve here in Germany. It is true that many of our investments were already planned before the change of government. The important message for me is that we are investing here in Germany as a company. We're creating new jobs. We're also confident that we can hold our own here as a location in global competition. We're willing to change to achieve this. Since 2022, Siemens Energy has been investing nearly EUR 1 billion at its German sites. We are planning for more investments here as well. Last year alone, we created 1,300 additional jobs in Germany. In the next fiscal year, we plan to hire another 1,500 new employees here in Germany. We train young people. We hire them.
Like many other German companies, we are doing this very single-mindedly, both the small and medium-sized enterprises and the large corporations as well. I think, therefore, that it is right that the new federal government now has set itself the goal of seeking closer cooperation with businesses in Germany. The government has a responsibility to create structures so that those investments pay off, especially also in comparison to other countries, because businesses will only invest in Germany if they find reliable overall conditions and intact infrastructure, competitive production costs, and well-trained personnel. If businesses like ours can support policymakers in any way to create these conditions, we're happy to do that because we all care about Germany as a business location. Now back to you, Tim. Thank you very much.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Thank you very much, Christian Bruch and Maria Ferraro.
You now have the possibility, journalists, to ask your questions. A technical remark: you can ask the questions in person if you've dialed in by phone. You receive the dial-in data with the invitation. If you want to ask a question, please press asterisk and 1. You can ask your questions in the chat. To avoid feedback, you should switch off the webcast now unless, of course, you only speak English. Of course, you can listen to the translation into English. You can ask your questions either in English or in German. The answer will be given in the same question. Asterisk 1 for a question. Now we'd like to ask you for the first question. We have a question from chat from Ed Ballard from The Wall Street Journal.
Mr. Bruch, you talked about the increased demand in the United States. He wants to know if the demand for gas turbines is so great in the U.S. that it would go beyond the investments that you have already announced when you talked about the investments and the expansions there.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Should I answer in English or German?
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
You can answer in German. It will be interpreted into English. Okay. Whatever's easier.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Good. Then I'll answer in German. Well, that might be a possibility. It will depend on how stable this high demand is. As you might know, today, we are manufacturing in the U.S., the blades, for example. In Florida, we produce this for the global market, not just the United States. As you know, we have structures in the United States. We have plants in the U.S.. We can also expand capacities. We'll take a very careful look at that.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
As I said, that's what we're doing right now. It's, of course, a question: will this demand remain stable and at that high level? Would we invest in the United States? Right now, we're investing about a half a billion dollars in plant expansions in the United States. It has become a key market. We want to be successful there. Thank you very much.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
The next question, Christoph Steitz from Reuters. Good morning, Mr. Steitz.
Christoph Steitz
Chief Company News Correspondents, Reuters
I have three questions. Mr. Bruch, you talked about a mid-double-digit figure for tariffs impacts. Is that the order of magnitude that you can expect every quarter? Will we have this amount every quarter? That's my, of course, question. The second question: what about the discussions with customers in the United States? You talked in the past about stability and the expectations on the horizon. Is this something that is reflected in your discussions with the customers? Order backlog. You've been chasing records after record every single quarter for as long as I can remember. How high can order backlog become without losing its health? I know that this has been something that you've been paying a lot of attention to. That's it. That's my question. Those are my questions for the time being.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Good morning, Mr. Steitz. Thank you for your questions. First of all, what about the tariff impacts? Where does this come from, primarily from longer, older service contracts? This is something the burden and the charges will mean. How long will these service contracts last? The contracts for new components or new gas turbines, new transformers, we can pass on the tariff effects there.
I assume that next year, we will have similar orders of magnitude. Over the course of the years, this will go down because from the service contracts, of course, we will successively come to an end. They'll be replaced by new ones. I'd like to mention one more thing. These tariff effects, don't consider this only EU-U.S.. The steel tariffs have an impact. Mexico, Canada, other countries also have an impact. This is something that is moving all the time. I have to be a bit cautious here in mentioning any old figure. I think we have to take a very careful look at this because it's complex and changing. Discussions with customers and new plants, especially Gas Turbines and Grid Technologies, this is driven by the question: can you deliver? This is something that we've done very successfully.
We can present this very successfully. That's why we have very good order intake. Of course, we can also pass on the tariff effects. You shouldn't forget one thing. These effects also impact other suppliers just as they affect us. We're no different from the others. At the end of the day, it means that the prices will go up. That's why we have to see how things developed when it comes to critical infrastructure. Our discussions with customers have been driven more by the question as to delivery times and not so much by the tariffs.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Thank you, Christoph, for the question regarding order backlog alike, not chasing records. I think it's really important. This is something that I stress quarter-over-quarter. It's not just about the growth of the order backlog. It's absolutely about the quality of that backlog.
What we indicate quarter after quarter is not only are we growing in the backlog, but that the margin quality continues to expand and be better in the backlog. I think that's absolutely a function of what we call internally of selectivity. Of course, we don't just book an order to book an order. We're selective in those orders. Also, secondly, because of the pricing power that, of course, we're able to have due to the market momentum. You're fully right. It's not just about increasing the order backlog. It's ensuring that the margin in that backlog continues to improve. That's exactly what we're seeing.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Next question from WirtschaftsWoche Clara Thier. Good morning, Ms. Thier. Can we have your question, please?
Clara Thier
Business Editor, WirtschaftsWoche
Yes. Hello. Good morning. I have a couple of questions on Gas Services. Now, first of all, are the numbers always referring to Gas Services or all of your businesses that you've mentioned when you talk about the quarterly figures? How full or how booked is your order book for Gas Services, how many years, in other words? What is the markup you can charge in the gas business in the U.S.? Can you tell us what your overall assessment is of the situation of tariffs, not only generally in the U.S. but also globally? How much of that is affected by that situation? Do you also see picking up demand in other countries? Now, the first question, Mr. Bruch, are we posting a record also at Gas Services when it comes to orders? That was the first question.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Okay. Now, I have to think now. I think it was the second highest order intake per quarter. Still, it's a special situation. Currently, they were seeing here in the market. Why? Because there are many customers that are buying more than one gas turbine, so multiples. It's not only about data centers, you mentioned that, but about 60% of our demand is the usual business. That would be coal to gas, oil to gas, that sort of conversion, or normal electricity growth. About 40% is new applications, so either data centers but also applications like what do you use the powerships, so floating the power stations that can be used for emergency or crisis situations or take LNG electrification, that sort of thing. This is now also what we're seeing. They're gaining importance. The share of data centers, well, let me be very clear.
The U.S. are dominating when it comes to demand for data centers. 40% of our gas turbines are related to the data center business. Globally, that figure stands at about 25%. Of course, we are talking here about, though, large-scale data centers, so hundreds, multiples of hundreds of megawatts. You would find that in regions of the world where electricity prices are low or plannable. Now, you would expect the United States with the hyperscalers. What we also now see is the Middle East. Again, this happens a bit later with a lag. I think that's the next big wave. Europe is a bit reticent about that. I think that was the questions. When will you be fully booked, as it were, with your orders? Well, delivery times are growing now. We are booked until 2027.
2028 already has good order backlog. If I remember correctly, 21 gigawatts of reservations is what we currently have. We have customers who are interested. At the same time, in the coming year and then also in 2027, we are going to see our capacity enlargements here. We're trying to balance our operations that well. What this means is we're in a good situation. Our planning horizon is very stable.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Okay. Next question will be in English. Plechinger from EnergyWatch. Christian, you need to answer in English. Please, Maz, fire your question.
Maz Plechinger
Journalist, EnergyWatch
Good morning. I didn't get the last part, Tim. You're welcome to answer in Danish as well. I have a few questions about Siemens Gamesa. One is regarding tariffs. You mentioned mid-double-digit euro effects. Why is that?
Which projects do I saw the Virginia senator talk about that they would have to pay around EUR 300 million in tariffs? Is it projects like those which have something in the contract that make you pay tariffs? That's one question. The other is regarding the onshore successor of the 5.X platform rather than a relaunch. Why is this a successor? How much is this indeed a new platform? Also, when do you expect sales to pick up? Thank you.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
If you can also turn to Danish. No, I probably do it in English. That's probably better for the rest. First of all, the tariffs. It's a mixed picture. Keep in mind, we have service, onshore, and also offshore execution at the moment in the U.S.. There's, obviously, also tariffs on steel, which is an element.
It's not just European Union and the U.S.. It's a mixed bag of these different things. Service is mainly local. I mean, that is something where there's the least impact between offshore and, obviously, some pieces of the onshore businesses where we import. That is what's driving the impact. On the successor, that's a super question. It will not be in the market under 5.X. It will be called 7.0. It shows you it's somewhere between a progression of the old platform and really some revised elements. However, let's say, obviously, we base it on things which have worked and which we know. We also, obviously, keep a prototype running while we start gradually to introduce the product. It is definitely not just 5.X with fixes.
It's really a renewed product, however, obviously, based mainly on the same frameworks. I think the team did a great job to really redesign it. It gives me a comfort that this can be a successful platform in the market.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Vielen Dank. Die nächste.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Thank you very much. Next question comes from Markus Frühauf from FAZ. Good morning, Mr. Frühauf.
Markus Frühauf
Business Correspondent, FAZ
Good morning. I hope you can all hear me.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
We hear you well.
Markus Frühauf
Business Correspondent, FAZ
I'd like to talk about your dividends because you said you talked about the early possibility to pay dividends and then. Ms. Ferraro earlier said 40% to 60% of net earnings are to be distributed. Is that also true for this year because you had a EUR 3 billion net profit? With Siemens India, you have special effect. It would be EUR 1.5 billion. What will be your reference for the dividend payment? I also have a question on the weak dollar. EUR 4 billion of negative FX, we heard, if I understand that correctly. How much is really the weak dollar weighing on your business and what that really means?
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Yes. I will absolutely go first. Thank you for the questions. Yes, let me clarify the dividend. The 40% to 60% is based on net income. The technical term is attributable to shareholders. Yes, that would be the range that we use also for this year. That would be the proposal that we would be put forward with that range for a dividend payment. Again, what I wanted to stress is it's for fiscal year 2025, but, of course, would only be paid after in February 2026 onwards, after the AGM approval.
That is the basis. You're correct there. With respect to the EUR 4 billion of FX, maybe let me clarify. That was relating to a translation effect in our order backlog. In other words, our order backlog stands at EUR 136 billion. Actually, if it wasn't for that translation effect, we would be closer to the EUR 140 billion. It did have an effect. Again, that's temporary in nature. It's something that we do every period. That's why it's called accumulative translation effect. Of course, that then would vary with the changes in the FX. What I do want to say is with respect to profit. Again, it's important to note that we are hedged. This is something that we do very methodically, especially for our projects.
With respect to profit, we are heavily hedged to ensure that we don't have that variability on a month-by-month or quarter-by-quarter basis.
Markus Frühauf
Business Correspondent, FAZ
The question about the respective dividend, is import to Siemens Energy, not India, right?
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Of course. Yes. If that was what was asked, yes, absolutely. It would be the Siemens Energy net income effect. I think what they were referring to is the special effect of EUR 473 million. That is deemed a special effect. Of course, it would be excluding that or could be excluding that profit because it's a non-cash effect to be technical.
Markus Frühauf
Business Correspondent, FAZ
Thanks.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Mr. Bruch. Mr. Frühauf. Mr. Bruch, he also asked the question about why you have the dividend ban that you've to not release just the dividend, that no longer a ban on the dividend.
Markus Frühauf
Business Correspondent, FAZ
That's a nice question. Well, okay. Let me try and give you the answer. The ban on paying out a dividend was really a major problem for our investors. In the next calendar year or the next fiscal year, the ban on the bonus will also be lifted. For this calendar year sorry, for this fiscal year, I should put it, that is still the way it is.
Christoph Meyer
Seasoned Foreign Correspondent, DPA
The next question is Christoph Meyer from dpa. Good morning, Mr. Meyer. Good morning. I would like to know this is a question of the strong position and high new orders. You have a very important and strong position on the market. How much does this influence the prices? Can you ask for better prices considering the high demand? How much does that amount to? Then another request.
Could you really tell us what about the EUR 1 billion or up to EUR 1 billion organically in operations in terms of profit? How much of this close to EUR half a billion can be added, considered for India? I assume that in this current fiscal year, you will be above last year's, especially driven by special items. Is that being far too speculative?
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Well, let me say something on the prices. Maria can talk about the net income. Well, let me put it this way. Generically speaking, in all areas, the orders that we take in, these are accretive to the backlog margin. In other words, profitability in the backlog is increased. Everything that we see in the prices is higher than the average. This is based on the price increases during the quarter.
We have been able to say that what we see now in gas turbines, we continue to have a situation where price increases can be achieved but not to the same extent as was the case in previous years or in previous quarters. The price curve is flattening out. A similar situation in Grid Technologies. This, as in gas, depends on the delivery dates. We also have to say, if you have a short-term delivery, and then you can enforce high price increases. If it's an order that will not go through until 2028 or 2029, then that's not the case. You have to see it that way. I think the most important message here is that everything that we take on board can increase the profitability of the backlog. In other words, the average profitability is improved as a result.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Let me take then the dividend question. Let me clarify again. You're fully right. Our guidance says around EUR 1 billion in net income for this fiscal year for Siemens Energy. We excluded in that guidance a special effect coming from the demerger of the Siemens Energy India Ltd. We now know this quarter that that effect is approximately EUR half a billion. We still maintain the EUR 1 billion. We don't include that in our guidance. Of course, the net income, including that impact, is exactly right. It's about the EUR 1.5 billion all in. Just two topics there with respect to what would we consider with respect to the dividend. Our dividend policy does indicate that, of course, we can exclude non-cash items. To be very clear, the Siemens Energy India Ltd, let's say, translation effect is a positive effect.
It's non-cash in nature. It's really a technical accounting treatment effect. Hence why we excluded it from our guidance accordingly. Again, our policy does indicate that we can exclude non-cash items. What I would ask is that we finish the fiscal year, determine how our net income fares, and then we go from there. Hopefully, that clarifies that.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Vielen Dank. Nochmal.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Thank you very much. If you want to ask a question, asterisk 1. We have 2 more questions in the chat. Mr. Bruch, a question from Ed Ballard from The Wall Street Journal. Let me read it out to you in English. Maybe you can answer in English. Administration indicated to Siemens Energy that additional manufacturing capacity for gas turbines would be desirable given the strength of demand growth.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
First of all, it's ourselves, not the traveling space, and seeing the good market. As I said, we have an interest to expand our production capacity in the U.S.. For the transformer, switchgears, we're doing it at the moment. For the blades factory in Florida, we are doing this at the moment. We are exploring further opportunities. What we are trying to balance out is also the understanding of what does the investment cost. You see the inflation in the construction market. Obviously, building a factory gets more and more expensive. We obviously try to understand what is really the long-term trajectory of the market going forward in the U.S.. We are in close contact also with the administration. Keep in mind, in a lot of cases, the state is even more relevant than the federal government.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy
Obviously, what is in interest, and I myself have been in Washington lately, is are we able, really, to ensure the supremacy in artificial intelligence by supplying the electricity? Absolutely, we are interested to contribute where we can and ensure that the U.S. is successful on their journey. In that regard, we continue to look into this and also discuss with the states and with the federal government in terms of how do they look on it, particular since the data center infrastructure is obviously linked also to certain federal decisions in terms of what comes when. We are in contact. I really want to underline that it's really market-driven for us from the customers. We will continue to look onto further investments in the U.S.. We are on it already.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Die nächste Frage.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Next question from the chat is from Joachim Herr of Börsen-Zeitung.
Joachim Herr
Veteran Journalist and Editor, Börsen-Zeitung
Mr. Bruch, you said before that tariffs are mostly affecting existing long-term service contracts. I don't know if Maria or Christian wants to take that. What are the effects of U.S. import tariffs in the coming years once those long-term service contracts expire?
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Well, first of all, tariffs affect everything. Okay. The question is, how much of it can we pass on to our customers or not? In that context, I do believe that tariffs will lead to a change in pricing structure. You are going to see higher prices also because our competitors are exactly in the same situation here. The question is, will you do more localization or not?
We'll very much hinge on how much you can plan this situation and how long-term that situation. No one is going to build a factory for the market in the next three or four years, right? Investments into a manufacturing facility are massive. Therefore, you need to have a feeling how a market develops over the next 10 years. That's really what matters. In that context, it's true that we're very much preoccupied with the tariff situation. I'd like to call on everyone, stay calm, look at the market, try to understand the underlying trends. That will be what matters most.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Thank you very much. Clara Thier from WirtschaftsWoche has a follow-up question. Miss Thier, go ahead.
Clara Thier
Business Editor, WirtschaftsWoche
Thank you very much. Follow-up question on Gas Services. Now, I've seen that your target was that by 2030, your gas emissions or Gas Services emissions are to be reduced by one-third. Is your climate target still up to date? If it is up to date, how do you want to achieve that while you at the same time are growing your orders and you grow your capacities in Gas Services? How do you stick to your target?
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Well, Scope 3 referred to the entire company. Let me say that at the top. It depends on how much customers switch to other fuels, right? I mean, that's what it was about there. If you're operating a gas turbine, you can fire it with hydrogen. This is why it's not that we have control of on our own. Now, obviously, we're looking at the situation as we speak.
Of course, it will be influenced by growth going forward. Again, let us also point out it doesn't depend on how we are developing but how the customer market is developing and if or when society is ready to invest into alternative fuels. Countries will have to spend money on that. This is something that is discussed across the board now. It's the truth of the matter that in any electricity system, you need dispatchable power. Dispatchable power means you can control flexibly the need. You can use a gas turbine, whether it takes natural gas or hydrogen, is your decision. We cannot resolve that on our own. In that sense, I cannot give you a final answer. We're trying to understand the market drivers as we see them out there.
What is important for me is that at the end of the day, everything is a Scope 1 emission. Everything that we do. Scope 3 refers to the investments carried out by others, not by us. Therefore, we will stick with our roadmap to reduce our Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions and to achieve net zero emissions by 2030 that we're striving for. That's my corridor, right? That's what I can influence. Looking at what the market does is hard for us to influence.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
Maz Plechinger from EnergyWatch. Maz, please.
Maz Plechinger
Journalist, EnergyWatch
Thanks for giving me another opportunity, Stell. Thank you for adding more details on the new onshore turbine. Could I get you to elaborate a bit more on its market potential, more specifically in the German market? How much of a difference do you assume that this turbine can make in the German market before the current boom begins to fade? Thanks.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy
Once again, an excellent question. I will probably be better able to tell you six months from now when I've seen, really, the sales teams having developed or starting to develop a project with the customers. What I hear from the, let's say, early discussions and pre-discussions which we had with customers across Germany, also across Northern Europe, also in areas we could consider like Australia is a very positive reception in terms of a high interest of customers in this turbine. Whether they order the turbine at the end, it's something where I really would like to see the proof points first from the market. I really have to say, I cannot tell you at this point in time.
I think the product itself is well positioned. Now we have to see how the customers are taking it up in the current environment. Obviously, yes, we would love to tap into the German market as well. As you know, project development in the German market takes particularly long because of the process and how it is. I would not expect that Germany is the first market what we see by taking in orders.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Gut. Damit sind alle Fragen beantwortet.
Tim Proll-Gerwe
Head of External Communications, Siemens Energy
All the questions have been answered. We've learned that Mr. Bruch speaks Danish as well. We can conclude today's press call. Thank you for joining us and for your interest. If you have any follow-up questions, my press team and myself will be happy to hear from you by phone.
The conference call for analysts with Christian Bruch and Maria Ferraro will begin at 10:30 AM. You can dial in if you like, but you can't ask questions. That's only for analysts. You can find the link on our website. The next date is our annual press conference. The year has gone by quickly. It will be on 14 November in Berlin. We'll send you out a save-the-date in the near future. Thank you all very much. That concludes today's conference call. Have a lovely day. Thank you very much.
[Unknown Speaker]
Unknown Speaker
Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, die Pressekonferenz ist nun beendet. Wir bedanken uns herzlich für Ihre Teilnahme und wünschen Ihnen einen angenehmen Tag. Auf Wiederhören.

content.text:
Operator
There won't be all that many surprises because we published our preliminary figures on 23 January. Today you'll be getting the full picture, and we'll be focusing on current topics such as the power plant strategy. Here with us in the room today, we have the CEO, Christian Bruch, and the CFO, Maria Ferraro. Christian Bruch will give you an overview of the past quarter, and then the CFO, Maria Ferraro, will give details on the Q1 figures. After that, as usual, both will be available to answer your questions. Mr. Bruch will be speaking in German, Ms. Ferraro in English. There'll be two webcasts, one for the original, where you will hear the original, and then the English line, where you will hear the English interpretation, and Ms. Ferraro will be transmitted in the original.
Following the QA, journalists will have a separate telephone number where they can sign up, and we sent you the link with the invitation for today's call. You can also sign up for this telephone dial-in today. If you are in the webcast and in the telephone line, then please put yourselves on mute in the telephone line so we don't have any feedback. The presentation can be downloaded on our homepage. Please remember there won't be a written speech today. Both will be speaking freely. I'd just like to remind you of our safe harbor statement on forward-looking statements, and this can be found on page two of our quarterly presentation. I'd like to hand over now to Christian Bruch, our CEO.
Christian Bruch
President and CEO, Siemens Energy AG
Thank you, Tim. Also, good morning. As Tim already said, the surprise today was certainly not too big. We already published our figures on 23 January. The reason for this was, as you know, that there were shifts between the quarters. This is a project-based business with a certain volatility and in an extremely dynamic market environment in energy. It's not always easy to plan specifically according to quarters, and we decided to early on inform the market about the good Q1. We have to say this, we had a very good start, good beginning of the year across all of the segments, particularly Gas Services, Grid Technologies, and Transformation of Industry that stand out with very, very good order intakes.
We have a record order intake of EUR 15.4 billion, and we assume that H1 will be stronger than H2. At the end of the day, you see that energy is a good and dynamic business segment and is growing considerably. Revenue amounted to EUR 7.6 billion. All segments contributed, very strong increase in Grid Technologies due to the strong order intake that we had in 2023, and Maria will, as usual, go into more detail with the figures. The profit before special items increased considerably to EUR 208 million. In Q1 of last year, it was EUR -282 million. This is a positive development as well.
As expected in Q1, we also had special items of EUR 1.6 billion that we were able to record. This is due to the sale of the 18% stake in Siemens Limited in India. Siemens Energy's earnings in Q1 amounted to around EUR 1.9 billion. Overall, I can say we're on track to achieve our targets for the year as a whole. We're working through the individual topics quarter by quarter. We have opportunities in the energy business and try to translate that into profitable growth. The other topic that we will continue to focus on are the quality problems or the solutions to the quality problems at Siemens Gamesa and at the same time, ramping up the production in the offshore business.
We know that we need to reestablish some of the confidence in the market. We're all working on this, step-by-step, and every quarter, we want to give you the opportunity to see what we are doing, what's happening. I'd like to say that working through all of these issues takes time. We want to do this with conscientiousness and diligence. I understand that there are questions how fast, how quick, how concrete, and whether we can be more precise. We try to balance this, and we're doing this step-by-step. Please understand that the technical studies have mostly been concluded. What does that mean?
Well, it means that the problems are being understood, and now what has been considered so far continues to be right. We continue to believe that they're right. Let me just put it into context again. You know that the provisions will be spent over the course of the next years. The biggest cash out is planned for 2025, but it all depends on the plans. As far as the offshore business is concerned, it's about ramping up the production, guaranteeing the ramp up of the production and working through the order backlog. Last year, we said that there were challenges in three areas. First, the disruption of the supply chain.
Secondly, the overly optimistic planning of the ramping up of the factories with the simultaneous introduction of new models, technologies, longer blades, and bigger cabins. That is something where we needed to try a few things before we can increase productivity. The third was the capacity expansion of the individual plants. Now we have achieved a lot regarding the supply chains. They've become more resilient. We've introduced more suppliers, additional suppliers. We've also bundled our procurement volumes in a more long-term way to cover the plans. When you look at the cash flow of Siemens Gamesa, you see that we've built up a little bit of stock. This is related to the offshore order backlog. We are addressing the issues from a construction point of view.
We've increased the capacities for the plants and have almost completed this. There are still individual aspects that need to be terminated, but now it is about step-by-step improving the processes in manufacturing. We need to focus on this, and as I said, this is a gradual process. The big ramp up is expected to take place in Q2 of the year. We're now introducing the new models, and the teams now need to be trained and improved, and the processes need to be improved. All we can say is it is happening step-by-step, and that's what we're focusing on. The next big issue last year was the counter guarantees from the federal government, the bank consortium, and the counter guarantees with the federal government have been signed now.
The agreement on EUR 11 billion that were signed by commercial banks based on the counter guarantee of the federal government has already entered into force. We do have the government guaranteeing EUR 7.5 billion as a counter guarantee. In addition to this, there will be an additional EUR 1 billion that has been guaranteed from three commercial banks. I always like to stress this because I'm being asked this repeatedly. It is a counter guarantee. It is a tool that is used for performance and payment measures. It is not a direct support, a direct subsidy from the state. We're paying a lot of fees to the state for this counter guarantee. I'd like to say this repeatedly because there is a big misunderstanding when it comes to that.
At the same time, we concluded the sale of the 18% share of Siemens Limited in India. I've already mentioned this, and I'd like to say thank you very much explicitly to Siemens AG for the fast and easy cooperation. These structures are anything but easy. It was difficult to do this, and it was great help for us that Siemens AG focused on this. We already announced this last year. We are progressing with regard to the focusing of the core business of Siemens Gamesa. One aspect of this is the sale of a 32% participation in the company Windar Renovables. This is a company that predominantly builds towers for wind mills. This is not a focus of us. The sale has been sold now.
The sale has been completed, but we continue to work with Windar, and we're also working on the integration of the central functions between Siemens Gamesa and Siemens Energy, as it was originally stipulated in the merger. We are working on achieving the originally communicated synergy goals. I'd like to mention a couple of examples. What I'm happy about when it comes to this is that we have not had any problems finding good examples in none of the quarters. That's always a positive sign. It shows that the energy market is both very, very dynamic and also that we have a good portfolio. Let me pick out two examples. One is our power plant project in Kazakhstan.
This is another project where old coal-fired power plants are being replaced by gas turbine power plants and cogeneration plants in the Kazakh capital of Almaty. You know that until 2030, Kazakhstan wants to reduce its greenhouse emissions by 25%. Coal continues to be an important fossil fuel in Kazakhstan, so such a project plays an important role in addition to other energy projects that are being discussed in Kazakhstan. Second example is from the strongly growing business unit, Grid Technologies, Viking Link. It's an HVDC link, high voltage direct current connection between the United Kingdom and Denmark. It's an almost 800km long underwater cable to ensure the exchange of power and ensure that there is guaranteed power for 2.5 million households.
This is an example for the projects that we can see everywhere in the order intake of Grid Technologies now. The nice thing about this project is that it was taken into operation three years after the work started. This shows that projects can be concluded quickly in the grid sector, and this is necessary for the energy transformation. One more thing I'd like to mention before I give the floor to Maria. It's the general market environment. At the Capital Market Day in November, we already said the market environment continues to be good. We do, with a certain level of concern, look at the Suez Canal geopolitical conflicts. In general, energy is an issue that currently sees an immense signal upswing. We see a positive demand at the global level.
At COP28 in Dubai, the discussions also stated that despite the good progress, the expansion, the speed of the expansion in the grid, particularly when it comes to renewable is not enough. There were declarations in Dubai focusing on tripling the capacity for renewable energies at the global level and doubling energy efficiency. Today, when it comes to the expansion until 2030, we are in a corridor where we can achieve 2.5, an increase of 2.5, when it comes to capacity. We're on the right track, but it needs to improve. You need to see that the big share of the expansion is taking place in China. China is ahead. Other regions in the world are slightly lagging behind. We'll now have to see that the expansion gets the necessary speed it needs.
If we look at wind power in Germany, we've made a lot of strides forward, but we haven't yet reached the speed necessary in order to achieve our goals at the end of the day. I think it is positive that we now have some basic pillars in the power plant strategy that were communicated, for example, that there will be a capacity market, among other things, that before the capacity market is introduced, there will have to be tenders for natural gas power plants that can then be switched to hydrogen. The third thing I think is positive is that hydrogen and promoting hydrogen has been removed from the back burner again. This is an impulse that is needed. That's the right analysis.
Now it's about putting the details into practice. How is it financed from the side of the government? How does it look like in concrete terms in 2024? We really have to go into the tenders. The global market is very tight as far as demand is concerned, so it's important to get moving here. This was a first important step. Now I'd like to give the floor to Maria for the figures.
Maria Ferraro
CFO, Siemens Energy AG
Thank you, Christian. Good morning, everyone. A warm welcome also from my side. Thank you for joining us today. Let me get right into our financial performance in Q1. Of course, as Christian mentioned, you already saw our preliminary numbers, which we published on 23 January. Today, I want to give you some more insights, perhaps starting with our performance at the group level. We did have a solid start to the year, and we continue to see positive momentum across all our former GP businesses. Siemens Gamesa performed within our expectations in Q1. Our order development was outstanding, better than expected, reflecting the continuous favorable demand pattern that we see in our markets. We also did benefit from some pull-forward effects in certain businesses. Looking at growth, it stands at 24% comparable despite a high basis of comparison.
This has resulted in orders for this quarter of EUR 15.4 billion. This is the highest ever order intake in a quarter to date. The book-to-bill ratio is very strong at slightly above two. This again is driving growth in our order backlog to a new high of EUR 108 billion. Revenue also grew significantly with almost 13% increase on a comparable basis. What's important is all segments contributed to this growth. The biggest contribution is coming from our Grid Technologies business. Service revenue also had a very strong start to the year and helped us here. This grew slightly more than the new unit business, and it is important also that we had a very strong service season across all business areas. Profit before special items did improve to EUR 208 million.
All of our business areas either improved or stayed at prior year's level. Our profit margin before special items came in at 2.7%. Special items, as already mentioned, included the pre-tax gain from the sale of our 18% stake in Siemens Limited India, as already indicated to you, of around EUR 1.7 billion, which brings us to the profit for the quarter of EUR 1.9 billion and a net income of EUR 1.6 billion. Free cash flow pre-tax came in at EUR -283 million. This is a bit of a mixed picture where we had positive contributions from our former GP businesses, supported by the higher profitability as well as, of course, with a high order intake value. You also get advanced payments from our customers.
This was offset by the negative free cash flow as expected at Siemens Gamesa of EUR -1.2 billion. At Siemens Gamesa, as I just mentioned, it's very important to note that this is seasonal in nature. The high cash outflow was, of course, expected and is as a result of the losses and seasonality as mentioned, where we're building up operating net working capital to of course ensure that we're able to convert our backlog in that business and the ramp up, of course, in our offshore business. Now, just maybe perfect segue into the next slide, looking at our order backlog. Of course, what's important here as always is that our order backlog really does provide us with visibility on revenue and conversion well beyond a 12-month timeframe.
In Q1, the backlog continued to grow, as mentioned, to a new record high of EUR 118 billion. We mentioned this at the capital market day in November, where we provided new midterm targets for all our business areas. The margins, this is what's important. The margins that we see in our order backlog are supporting these targets, and we continue to see a positive progression also in Q1 within our backlog. What's also important is close to 50% of the backlog is service business, and this of course provides us with excellent visibility for future recurring resilient revenue with high margins and of course good cash conversion.
We're also seeing strong growth in our new units business, and this is also important, of course, as we continue to grow our installed base and new units help us create additional service revenue in the future. Again, the backlog is important and it's excellent that it's growing, but we need to continue to convert that into profitable revenue over the years to come. Looking at the next page, our liquidity, our return to a net cash position. As you know, we proactively initiated measures to strengthen our balance sheet with significant near-term cash measures, targeting EUR 2.5 to 3 billion cash inflows by means of the acceleration of our existing divestment program and including the sale of the 18% stake in Siemens Limited India to Siemens AG.
Just to repeat, we closed the sale of the 18% stake in Siemens Limited India to Siemens AG early December. This resulted in a cash inflow of roughly EUR 2.1 billion in cash and a one-time P&L gain of close to EUR 1.7 billion. Again, you notice the difference between the profit gain here and the cash inflow from the transaction. This is due to the existing book value we had for the Siemens Limited India share investment. The profit booked in special items represents the gain made on that value. Overall, all things considered, our liquidity position remains strong. Our cash and cash equivalents at the end of the quarter grew to EUR 5.3 billion, while our financial debt shrank to EUR 3.9 billion, of which 3.2 therein is long-term in nature.
As a result, we returned to an adjusted net cash position of approximately EUR 840 million. This again is in line with our focus to maintain a strong balance sheet, which of course is underlying our commitment to maintaining an investment-grade rating. Now let's take a look at the business areas and start with Gas Services. Q1 was a very solid start for Gas Services. Orders exceeded last year's high level by 13.1%. This again driven by higher volume of large orders and the backlog then grew for GS to EUR 42 billion. Revenue grew by just shy of 11% on a comparable basis to EUR 2.7 billion, again against a very high prior year level.
Looking back, as I said earlier, with respect to the strong service performance, we had a favorable mix in business this quarter with both service and new unit business increasing here. Profit before special items came in very close to the strong level of last year's quarter at EUR 313 million or 11.7%. Moving to Grid Technologies, which also had a very strong start into the fiscal year. Here you see an outstanding order development that continues with the overall positive market environment for Grid Technologies. Orders in Q1 exceeded already the high level from prior year by just shy of 33% and rose to EUR 8.2 billion. This development was driven by GT's product business and HVDC orders in Germany, also in part benefiting from pull-forward effects.
The book-to-bill was just shy of four, and the backlog rose to EUR 28 billion. Revenue also grew substantially by just over 33% and came in at EUR 2.1 billion. This again, supported by the strong order intake conversion that we saw in previous years. Profit before special items came in strong at EUR 213 million. This is a 10.2% and significant improvement versus last year. Partly due again to our higher revenue, but also thanks to the higher margin in the process order backlog. Now let's turn to Transformation of Industry on the next page. Here, the focus on selectivity with improved price risk profiles and continued focus, which is key on executing with operational excellence and a focus on productivity. This is all nicely reflected in the Q1 results for Transformation of Industry.
Here we booked EUR 1.6 billion in orders in Q1. This is a 39% increase comparable to last year. The book-to-bill came in at 1.4, just over 1.4, and the backlog rose to EUR 7 billion. Revenue also grew significantly by just shy of 18% on a comparable basis, with all four independently managed businesses showing double-digit growth. Service also a contributing factor here, and we had a strong customer demand for year-end services. Profit nearly doubled to EUR 105 million with a corresponding margin of just over 9%.
This was driven by higher revenue, as just mentioned, but also by better pricing, and was also here, and we talked about that, we had some timing in shifts and project shifts, and here you saw that was particularly influenced by timing in products and projects, currency impacts, and as mentioned, quite a strong service start. Now moving on to our wind business, Siemens Gamesa. Looking at orders in Q1, this was slightly above prior level. In the onshore business, as you know and as fully expected, our orders were slightly halved due to the temporary suspension of sales activities for the 4.X and 5.X onshore turbines. However, this was made up by the strong growth in service orders and in offshore.
Revenue grew at just shy of 5% comparable, though we saw again the decline in onshore due to the known issues as just mentioned, and the offshore ramp up challenges.
